preamble: Debuccalization of the velar ejective: [kʼ] loses its oral closure and keeps only the glottal one, giving [ʔ]. Fallon (2002) counts this among the most frequent ejective changes, attested as regular or dialectal change in Chadic, Cushitic, Omotic, Athabaskan and Jicaquean. Several cases are still variable between dialects, showing the change in progress. Maltese, Cairene and urban Levantine Arabic reach ʔ in two steps, through uvular q (*kʼ > q > ʔ); each step is filed separately. In Khoe, the velar ejective affricate *kxʼ (kept in !Ora) was reduced to a glottal onset in Nama, with Griqua showing intermediate kʔ ~ ʔ. In Athabaskan, stem-final *kʼ became ʔ in Navajo (*tsʼakʼʸ 'dish' > tsʼaaʼ).

examples.note: Word-initial ƙ only (Dresel 1977, cited in Fallon 2002). The sources consulted give only this one example.
Western Jicaque kat instead lost the glottalization (Campbell & Oltrogge 1980).
Wikipedia (Jicaquean languages), table after Campbell & Oltrogge (1980); Western Jicaque kaw- lost the glottalization instead.
Same table; Western Jicaque has te-ga. Word-finally Tol keeps the ejective: *sokʼ 'tail' > Tol sokʼ.
Stem-final position; Central Ahtna tsʼaayʼ has a glottalized glide instead.
Source is the ejective affricate kxʼ (Proto-Khoe *kxʼ, Vossen 1997); Nama does not write the predictable initial [ʔ].
Griqua ʔani-b beside kʔani-s shows the intermediate stage.
